title: Braxton County: A vision for economic prosperity | | wvnews.com
text:
In the geography of West Virginia, Braxton County occupies a position of distinct advantage. Situated in the heart of the state and bisected by the critical artery of I-79, Braxton County is physically positioned to be a powerhouse of commerce and logistics.
Yet, for too many of our residents, the local economic reality has not matched the promise of our geography.
If we are to ensure that our families can build their futures here—thriving rather than merely surviving—we must move beyond passive optimism and embrace a bold, visionary strategy for economic development.
The data reveals the core of our challenge. While our unemployment rate, sitting at 3.3% as of May 2026, shows that our people are hardworking and employable, the quality of the jobs available remains a hurdle.
Braxton County’s average weekly wage of $1,026 falls significantly behind the West Virginia state average of $1,203 and is a long way from the national average of $1,569.
With approximately 4,901 people employed across the county, our goal must be clear: we need to elevate the “floor” of our economy by attracting industries that offer high-skill, high-wage opportunities.
The elements for this transformation are already in place. We often speak of “location, location, location,” and in Braxton County, that mantra isn’t just a cliché—it is our greatest asset.
Our access to I-79 offers immediate proximity to major markets, a logistical advantage that businesses crave. Braxton Co. has 37.5 Interstate miles with four major exits. Add in the connection for another four-lane highway U.S. 19 to Summersville, The New River Gorge and Beckley and we have another major artery pumping commerce through Braxton County.
When paired with our abundant developable land and rich natural resources, we possess the raw ingredients for significant industrial expansion.
However, attracting the right employers requires more than just land; it requires vision and “shovel-ready” investment. Meaningful economic development projects—focused on site development, broadband infrastructure, and industrial park expansion—must be our priority.
We must aggressively market our central location to industries that value reliable transit access and a workforce that is second to none. We cannot wait for opportunity to come to us; we must market what makes Braxton County the obvious choice for growth.
Furthermore, we must capitalize on our greatest differentiator: quality of life. In a post-pandemic economy, professionals and companies are increasingly prioritizing locations that offer a balance between work and the outdoors.
Our beautiful mountains, the vast expanses of Sutton and Burnsville Lakes, and the pristine reaches of the Elk River are not just recreational amenities—they are economic drivers.
They are the tools we use to recruit talent who want to trade the congestion of urban centers for the unmatched quality of life found in Braxton County.
Braxton County families deserve more. They deserve careers that provide the financial security to raise children here and the opportunity to retire here with dignity.
This vision requires leadership that is willing to build for the long term—investing in the infrastructure that invites high-paying industry while protecting the natural beauty that defines our home. This will require local, state and federal leadership working together.
